title: Unit final: trees
sub: New problems to recognize, a BST check trace, an in-order trap and explaining out loud
cards/0/q: New problems. Match the statement with the technique.
cards/0/pairs/0/0: The average node value on every level
cards/0/pairs/1/0: The length of the longest path between two nodes
cards/0/pairs/1/1: Return the height, update hl + hr
cards/0/pairs/2/0: The k-th smallest value in a BST
cards/0/pairs/3/0: The common ancestor of two nodes in a BST
cards/0/pairs/3/1: Walk down by key order, O(h)
cards/0/pairs/4/0: Is there a root-to-leaf path with sum target
cards/0/pairs/4/1: DFS passing the remaining sum down
cards/1/q: Find Bottom Left Tree Value (LeetCode #513): return the leftmost value on the last level of the tree. How?
cards/1/options/0: Level-order traversal: remember the first node of every level — after the loop it is the answer
cards/1/options/1: Go left from the root while there is a left child
cards/1/options/2: Level-order traversal, remembering the last node of every level
cards/1/explain: The first node of a level is the one taken first after reading queue.Count; the last one remembered is the leftmost on the last level. O(n) time, O(w) memory. There is also a trick: enqueue the right child before the left one — then the answer is the last node taken.
cards/1/wrong/1: The leftmost node of the tree is not necessarily on the last level: on [1, 2, 3, null, null, 4] going left stops at 2, but the answer is 4.
cards/1/wrong/2: The last node of a level is the rightmost: that is the right side view, and we need the leftmost.
cards/2/q: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree (LeetCode #1448): a node is good if no value on the path from the root to it is greater than its own. Count the good nodes; up to 10⁵ nodes. How?
cards/2/options/0: DFS passing the path maximum down: a node is good if val ≥ max
cards/2/options/1: Level-order traversal: a node is good if it is not less than the maximum of its level
cards/2/options/2: In-order: a node is good if it is not less than the previous one
cards/2/explain: The condition is about ancestors, and ancestors are the path from above. As with the interval in the BST check, a summary of the path travels down — here a single number, the maximum. Dfs(node, max): the count grows if node.val >= max, and the children get Math.Max(max, node.val). O(n) time, O(h) stack; for a chain of 10⁵ nodes, an explicit stack of (node, max) pairs.
cards/2/wrong/1: A level is neighbours, not ancestors: the level maximum says nothing about the path from the root.
cards/2/wrong/2: In-order neighbours are not ancestors: a node and the previous one in in-order may sit in different branches.
cards/3/task: A new tree: [8, 4, 12, 2, 6, 10, 14, 1, 3, 5, 9]. Step through the bounds check; the rig will stop twice and ask what happens next.
cards/3/goal/asks/0/q: The left subtree of 4 — nodes 2, 1, 3 — is fine. Next is 6, the right child of 4. What is the interval of 6?
cards/3/goal/asks/0/explain: Going right from 4, the bottom becomes 4, and the top stays what came to 4 — 8: this whole subtree is to the left of the root. (4, +∞) would forget the root — that is exactly the “compare only with the parent” mistake.
cards/3/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: 9 is inside (6, +∞) — fine, the tree is valid
cards/3/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: 9 is larger than its parent 6 — the right child is fine
cards/3/goal/asks/1/q: 5 ∈ (4, 6) — fine. The last node is 9, the right child of 6. What does the check say?
cards/3/goal/asks/1/explain: 9 receives (6, 8): the bottom is its parent 6, the top is the root 8. 9 > 8, although 9 lies to the left of the root. Against its parent 9 compares fine, so the “children only” check would call the tree valid. The root’s right subtree — 12, 10, 14 — is never checked.
cards/4/q: The k-th smallest in a BST. On the tree [5, 3, 6, 2, 4] with k = 1 this code returns 5 instead of 2. Tap the buggy line.
cards/4/explain: A node is counted before its left subtree — that is pre-order, so the root 5 is counted first. A BST reads in ascending order in-order: first Walk(node.left), then count the node, then Walk(node.right). The --k line belongs between the two calls.
cards/5/q: Checking “is it balanced”. The naive solution computes Height(left) and Height(right) with a separate recursion at every node. The one-pass solution returns the height or −1. What does it buy?
cards/5/options/0: O(n) instead of O(n log n) on an even tree: every height is computed once
cards/5/options/1: Nothing in time: both are O(n)
cards/5/explain: The naive one recomputes the heights of everything below at every level: on an even tree that is log n levels of n work — O(n log n). One pass hands the height to the parent, and −1 cuts the checks above short at once. Memory is the call stack in both, O(h).
cards/5/wrong/1: Height(left) is itself a walk of the subtree. Calling it from every node walks each node as many times as it has ancestors.
cards/5/wrong/2: The recursion stays — and so does the O(h) stack. The gain is in time, not memory.
cards/6/q: Unity: a scene has 10⁴ transforms, and two objects sit about 20 levels deep under the same root. You need their common parent. What do you do?
cards/6/options/0: Climb via parent: equalize the depths and step up together — tens of steps
cards/6/options/1: GetComponentsInChildren<Transform>() on the root and a recursive LCA over the tree — O(n)
cards/6/options/2: Breadth-first search from the root to both objects, then compare the paths
cards/6/explain: A Transform links to its parent, so the answer lies on two upward paths: depths of 20, equalizing and climbing — tens of steps and zero allocations. A top-down walk is only needed when there are no parent links, as with LeetCode’s TreeNode.
cards/6/wrong/1: That is a new array of every transform under the root and a walk of the whole subtree — for an answer that lies on two short upward paths.
cards/6/wrong/2: A top-down walk visits the whole subtree. Climbing via parent walks only two paths as long as the depth.
cards/7/q: You are solving Count Good Nodes out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/7/items/0: Clarify: is an equal value a good node? How many nodes, can the tree be empty
cards/7/items/1: Naive: for every node walk the path from the root again — O(n·h)
cards/7/items/2: Idea: pass the maximum of the path from the root down
cards/7/items/3: Write the code: Dfs(node, max), good if val ≥ max, children get Math.Max(max, val)
cards/7/items/4: Run [3, 1, 4, 3, null, 1, 5]: four good nodes — 3, 4, 5 and the lower-left 3
cards/7/items/6: Edge cases: a single node, all values equal, a chain of 10⁵ — an explicit stack
cards/7/explain: The same order as throughout the course: the problem, a baseline, the idea, the code while talking, a dry run, complexity, edge cases. The run shows that the 1 under the root 3 is not good, while the 3 under that 1 is: the maximum on its path is 3.
cards/8/q: Complexity of this unit’s solutions. What is true? Select all.
cards/8/options/0: Recursive MaxDepth is O(n) time and O(h) memory; on a chain h = n
cards/8/options/1: Level-order traversal is O(n) time with O(w) memory; on a complete tree w is about n/2
cards/8/options/2: The BST bounds check is O(n log n): the intervals narrow at every level
cards/8/options/3: LCA in a plain binary tree is O(h): we only go down one side
cards/8/options/4: The maximum path is O(n): each node returns a value once and updates best once
cards/8/explain: Every traversal in this unit visits each node once. Narrowing an interval is O(1) per node, so the BST check is O(n). Going down one side only works in a BST, where the key order decides; in a plain tree LCA does not know which way to go and walks both subtrees — O(n).
